These hon. gentlemen are supposed to be the instructors of the people, and if they would tell them the exact truth of this matter, there would be no adverse feeling in the province of British Columbia. These two provinces lie side by side and their interests are closely intertwined. The province of British Columbia is willing to take the agricultural products of the Northwest and pay fair prices for them, and the people of the Northwest Territories should prefer to take from the people of British Columbia the things they produce. If the lumber manufacturers of British Columbia could buy their hay, oats, beef and pork on the other side of the line, they would not I care for this duty, because the- prices would be so much less on account of the short haul that they could afford to compete with their rivals. But under present conditions they are handicapped, and they come to this court of last resort and ask for that justice which they in common with the people of every other province are entitled to receive at the hands of this parliament. I regret that the hon. Minister of Finance did not deem it his duty to say here and now, not waiting for the budget, that he would give them that justice. It would not have affected the price of lumber nor the conditions in any way injuriously for him to make that statement, so that we would not have great lumber mills like the Hastings mill closing down in British Columbia for the want of that measure of protection which the hon. member for New Westminister has asked for here to-day.

I wish in the first place to heartily congratulate the hon. member for New Westminster on bringing up this matter for the third time. I hope the hon. gentleman has been converted to the views he has preached today. If we are to judge from the hon. gentleman's former utterances on this question, we may conclude that he held convictions in one direction and held a brief in the other direction. That was precisely the condition of the hon. gentleman, I think, two years ago, when he declared in most emphatic terms that anything he might have said in urging the importance of a question similar to that which he has brought up to-day, was not to be taken as indicating in the slightest degree that he was a protectionist. In order that I may not do the hon. gentleman any injustice, I quote what he said. This is from ' Hansard ' of 1902, at page

1509. The bon. gentleman, after discussing the question with great eloquence and at some length, had this to say :
I think the country must have a tariff under the present conditions. I am not a proctection-ist, I never have been a protectionist, and when I go as far as I do, I do not think it is any evidence that X am a protectionist.
Is not that a very extraordinary declaration from a gentleman seeking protection here ? How are hon. gentlemen going to have an industry preserved against the inroads of foreign products when they only seek protection for a single locality ? These gentlemen are sectional protectionists. How does the hon. gentleman hope to get anything from the government he is supporting ? The hon. gentleman comes here with a brief from his constituents, he talks against his own convictions, and he asks the Minister of Finance to take into consideration a matter of great importance. I think I can without great difficulty imagine what the views of the Minister of Finance are when that claim is so strongly urged. I can imagine that he meets the hon. gentleman in the corridor and says to him : You must make a show of protection for your province ; you must ask for so much on lumber; hut you quite understand that I am not going to give it to you ; and you must support the Liberal party. That is precisely what I think is in the mind of the Minister of Finance at this moment. But there is another singular feature, and it is this, that the hon. gentlemen who have been taking some part in this debate, the moment they have uttered their last sentence, have skuiked out of the chamber. They do not like to be confronted with their inconsistencies of the past. Let me take one or two of them. The hon. member for Alberta (Mr. Oliver), who is not in the chamber, and probably had some idea of what he had said in the past when the question of giving greater protection to horses in the Northwest Territories was brought up had this to say :
Now, as representing probably the largest and most populous agricultural constituency in this Dominion, I have no hesitation on this occasion in voting and taking sides with the rearers of horses as against the users of inferior horses.
That hon. gentleman was ready to support protection for horses. Then there is my hon. friend from Western Assiniboia (Mr. Scott). He disavowed every notion of protection but wanted horses protected on that occasion. This is what he said :
I may say it is not from the point of view of a protectionist, in the ordinary tariff sense,
that I support the plea of my hon. friend

-meaning the hon. member for Macdonald (Mr. Boyd). The hon. gentleman had an original way of obtaining protection for horses. He wanted them classed as pernicious literature. These are his own words : Mr. CLANCY.
The idea which I think should prevail in this matter is something similar to that which prevails in regard to the importation of pernicious literature.
That is what he had to say. There are occasions when the sincerity of hon. gentlemen are put to a test, and this is one of them, and the hon. member for Westminster will find that he cannot apply one rule in one case and another in another without having public attention drawn to it. On a former occasion there was a resolution introduced which gave these hon. gentlemen the hon. member for Westminster and his friends an opportunity of showing just where they stood. The resolution was as follows :
This House regarding the operation of the present tariff as unsatisfactory, is of opinion that this country requires a declared policy of such adequate protection to its labour, agricultural products

Including horses, of course.
-manufactures and industries as will at all times secure the Canadian market for Canadians.
How did the hon. member for Westminster vote on that occasion ? He voted agains.t that resolution. So did the hon. member for Western Assiniboia (Mr. Scott) and so did the hon. member for Burrard (Mr. Macpher-son), yet' all these hon. gentlemen are to-day asking protection for their different sections. Is it not time that an end should be put to this miserable farce ? I venture to say that after the hon. member for Westminister and the others have made vigorous speeches in favour of protection, they will be found turning their backs on that policy before the session is through. That is an assertion one can safely make. The Minister of Finance is not in his place, but the First Minister is, and we know that he has two policies, one for the east and one for the west. Where is the Minister of the Interior, who we have been told, put his back against the wall and would allow no protection for the west ? But so long as the right hon. gentleman has sufficient support in the east to maintain himself in office, he can allow his friends to quarrel and will be sure of their support, no matter what may happen. But the people have yet to speak, and the right hon. gentleman may find that he cannot afford to disregard the people.

If my hon. friend from Bothwell (Mr. Clancy) had followed my remarks, he would not have come to the conclusion that I made them with the sole purpose of getting a duty put on rough lumber. They were rather in support of the contention that the duty should be taken off mill machinery coming in from the United States, which we are obliged to import for our mills.

Does the hon. gentleman say that he did not advocate a duty on

rough lumber on that occasion and lead as well ?

The remarks to which my hou. friend refers that I made on the lead question, I adhere to just as strongly to-day. What I said then, I stand by now. We must have a measure of protection such as we advocate on this side, but I could not see the philosophy of having' an uneven tariff, for which there was no cogent reason.
I could not see why, if we have to pay duty on flour and other products of the Territories, the article of lumber should be allowed in free. Or if lumber be allowed in free, the duty should be taken off planing machines, saws, teeth and things of that kind which the lumbermen of British Columbia must buy in the United States and on which they have to pay duty of from 25 to 30 per cent. If you will not impose a duty of $2 a thousand feet on rough lumber, then take the duty off these articles.
What is it the hon. gentleman is asking the House to do ? Does he want the duty put on rough lumber or taken off machinery ?
If you will not put a duty on rough lumber, take it off the articles which go into the manufacture of lumber.
Which does the hon. gentleman advocate ?
It is immaterial to us which is done. In either case we would be in a better condition than that in which we are now.

What advantage would it be to the. Hastings Lumber Company to have the duty taken off machinery ?
ill'. MORRISON. It would enable them to manufacture lumber much cheaper and compete in the American market.

If the Hastings Lumber Company have failed, it is because of the insufficient duty on coarse lumber. They have their plant. now, what good would it do them to reduce the duty on machinery ? I want to congratulate the hon. member for Burrard (Mr. Macpherson) who evidently has been reading the speech which the right hon. leader of the House made in Montreal. The right hon. gentleman there said that he was neither a free trader nor a protectionist but a practical man, and this gentleman from Burrard uses exactly the same language. We find that he is a protectionist in one place and a free trader in another. But the party to which I belong, I am glad to say, has a very pronounced policy. Its policy is adequate protection.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Hear, hear.

We believe in adequate protection, because it will benefit the whole country and are not in favour of imposing a duty to suit one particular constituency
and taking off a duty to suit some other constituency. I am not in favour of removing the duty from articles which are not manufactured in my constituency and imposing a duty on other articles which are manufactured there. We have had hon. members of this House from time to time declare themselves in favour of a united Canada. We are a nation formed out of several different provinces, by the amalgamation of which we become a united Dominion, and I ask how is it possible to have a united people if we find hon. gentlemen solely regarding our fiscal policy from the point oj view of divergent local interests. We have certain of these hon. gentlemen declaring against protection on certain articles while others favour such protection.
I would like to ask the hon. gentleman (Mr. Ingram) a question. How does he reconcile what he is now saying with the fact that his party took the duty off lumber in 1894 ?

I suppose that, after fair investigation they found that it was in the interest of the people to remove it. I presume they had imposed the duty for the same reason. But it is suggested to me, and I think the suggestion is a good one. that I should refer the hon. member (Mr. Morrison) to the hon. member for West Assiniboia (Mr. Scott) who, I understand, proved that the lumber duty was in the interest of the people. With respect to the duty on lumber,
I take the stand that, if the United States put on a high duty, we, on this side, if it is to our interest, should put on such a duty as will secure our market to [DOT] our manufacturers. I go further and say that if the great lumbering interests of British Columbia are suffering through an insufficient duty, then the government should increase the* duty so as to give them a fair chance to hold the market. To-day, we are told, members from the Northwest Territories are opposed to protection in this matter of lumber. Is it not the fact that the great lumbering industry of British Columbia is one of the greatest, if not the greatest industry in that province ? By the encouragement of the manufacture of lumber in British Columbia and the encouragement of the great mining industry of that province, the number of labourers employed will be greatly increased, and so a market will be provided for the produce of the Northwest Territories which will greatly benefit the agriculturists of that portion of the Dominion, for it is well known that the nearer the market the better for the producers. I am not afraid to have .that principle applied to the section that I represent. I am prepared to say to the Minister of Finance :	You represent a
province which has a large coal industry. It is true that in our section we have people who are interested in cheap soft coal, and who are even now petitioning to have the duty taken off soft coal. The people of Nova

Scotia accept duties upon agricultural products which are produced in the section of country from which I come, and so they contribute to the prosperity of the people I represent. I am Canadian enough to be willing, in return, to have duties imposed which shall benefit the coal industry of the province of Nova Scotia. And it is only by that means that we in Canada can succeed. If we take narrow views on questions of this kind we shall never be a united people, and, unless united we can never be great. I have been in this House time and time again when the attention of the right lion. Prime Minister had been drawn to the fact that in his own cabinet he had men some of whom entertained diametrically opposite views on the trade question. For my part, I have always believed ' that, under our system of government a cabinet must be united on broad questions of policy, and, unless united, the cabinet was not constitutionally formed. But we have seen certain members of the right lion, gentleman's cabinet go to one district and declare certain views on the subject, while another would go to another district and declare directly opposite views. And. when his attention was drawn to this fact the right hon. gentleman rather delighted in saying that that was how his cabinet was constituted- that it contained men who entertained all kinds of views, and, for that very reason they were a cabinet to be approved rather than condemned. If I am wrong in this statement, I would be very glad to be corrected ; but that is the inference I drew from what the right hon. gentleman has told us.
We have frequently heard it said that there is no protection to agriculturists in this country. I believe I am right in saying that the Postmaster General (Sir Win. Mulock) the hon. member for North Norfolk (Mr. Charlton) and others on that side were prepared to say, as against those Conservatives who claimed credit for the protection afforded to our farmers bv the duties on agricultural products, that 'these duties really afford no protection. If that statement is correct, then if these gentlemen are to be consistent they should remove these duties. If these duties were removed, we would see what opinion the farmers would express as to the effect of these duties in protecting their industry. I am quite prepared to state here that, if I had my way, I would increase the duty on many of the products of our farms, instead of diminishing those duties. Take, for instance, the case of horses. In 1902-3, we exported 1,900 horses to the United States, and upon those horses there was charged a duty of 271 per cent. On the other hand we imported from the United States over 29,000 horses, the duty charged on our side being only 20 per cent. Now, the people of this country, especially those of the Northwest can produce any quantity of horses. Is there any good Mr. INGRAM.
reason why we should not raise our duty to the figure of that imposed by the United States, 271 per cent ? There was a question that came up in the last election in the county of Lambton. The greatest industry of that county is cattle raising, and. notwithstanding that the people of Canada can produce more cattle than they can consume, we still allow cattle from the United States to be imported at a lower duty than that which is imposed upon cattle sent from this country to the United States.
I should say that on cattle, horses-I will go so far as butter, eggs and all the articles produced by the farmers of this country- we should place duty for duty against the United States, and I am sure it will be encouraging the agriculturists of this country, we will be helping and retaining the market for the farmers. This we are not doing now, by reason of the unequal and unfair tariffs between the two countries:	So far as the
manufacturers are concerned, they are in a position to speak for themselves, but I can go this far, that the Conservative party, in the matter of their conduct towards the manufacturers of this country, have always, since 1878, been loyal to the national policy, loyal to the protective policy, loyal to what we believe to be adequate protection for the manufacturing and all other industries of this country. And yet, (Sir. when an election cotnes on hon. gentlemen who do not believe in protection, go to the trusting manufacturers-because some manufacturers are trusting to this government - to-day and have been trusting for some years past. They go to them and tell them that if they support the Liberal party they will increase the duty or give greater protection than they have had. I regret to say that some of our manufacturers are prepared to take a sprat from thfi hon. gentlemen instead of supporting the party which is genuinely protectionist in this country. They are willing to take a sop from the hon. gentlemen opposite instead of supporting their friends who have been true and loyal to them ever since 1878. There will be another opportunity to discuss this on the budget, and I am sure that hon. gentlemen on this side of the House will have no two policies on this question. They will be loyal and true to protection, the course they have pursued ever since 1878.
Motion (Mr. Morrison) to adjourn negatived.
House in committee on Bill (No. 72) to amend the National Transcontinental Railway Act.-Sir Wilfrid Baurier.

I wish to ask the right hon. gentleman (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) whether or not he is able to give us the clause to which he referred last evening, when he said that the whole stock was a security for the operation of the eastern

section. My right lion, friend said that we would find that in the contract ; he had not ihe clause at the moment, but would give it to us later.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: If I said 'the whole stock,' I did not express my whole meaning. I meant the whole of the stock on the eastern division.
My hon. friend was referring to the rolling stock ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Oh, yes.
I thought he referred to the common stock.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I wish to refer to section 35 (c) :
A mortgage which shall be a charge upon the rolling stock constituting the equipment of the eastern division next after the charge mentioned in paragraph thirty-five (a) to secure to the government the rental payable in respect of the eastern division, the efficient maintenance and continuous operation of the said eastern division, and the observance and performance by the company of the terms of this agreement.
And also to section 25 :
The said lease shall also contain such other covenants and provisions, including proper indemnity to the government in respect of the working of the railway, as may be deemed necessary by the government to secure the proper carrying out of this agreement.
I misunderstood mv right hon. friend : I thought when he used the word ' stock,' omitting the word ' rolling '

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Hear, hear.
BORDEN-he was under the impression that the stock itself was pledged to the government.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The mistake was probably mine.

My right hon. friend also spoke in this way :
At all events the Grand Trunk have so much confidence in the enterprise that they are ready to lease the line and pay 3 per cent interest upon it. My hon. friend says that he will not discuss the financial aspect of the matter now, nor shall I. The Grand Trunk control this company. But my hon. friend says they put no money in it. They will have to put some money in it, otherwise they cannot fulfil the contract. At the present time if the enterprise is successful they have to pay 3 per cent for the lease. Why are the Grand Trunk willing to pay 3 per, cent on the lease ?
I would like to again call the attention of the right hon. gentleman to the fact that the Grand Trunk Railway Company has not to pay any rental ; that is merely a stipulation binding on the Grand Trunk Pacific.
1 understand my right hon. friend assents to that.
Sir WILFRID' LAURIER, Yes.
The Grand Trunk is not a party to the contract.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The covenant is with the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company, but my reasoning was that, although the contract was with the Grand Trunk Pacific Company, the Grand Trunk Company are bound to control the Grand Trunk Pacific Company, and therefore, indirectly, they assume the obligation.
They would not assume any obligation, any legal obligation.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: No.

I think that is quite clear. Then my right hon. friend referred to another matter. He said :
Of course my hon. friend may say that the Giand Trunk Railway can go to Chicago. So it can, but if it goes to Chicago it forfeits its rights under the contract, and it takes all the consequences.
In what way does the Grand Trunk forfeit its right by going to Chicago ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Legally, that would not apply ; but, inferentially, if the Grand Trunk Company were to go to Chicago, I do not see how they could carry their trade to Chicago by the American side and at the same time be able to implement this contract and pay the 3 per cent on the road. If they are going to pay the 3 per cent on the lease, they must earn it in some way, and in order to earn that money they must supply the traffic.
My right hon. friend (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) was not using forfeiture in a legal sense, but in a business sense.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Certainly not in a legal sense, but assuredly in a business sense.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Does not something depend in this connection on section 42 ?
It is hereby declared and agreed between the parties to this agreement that the aid herein provided for is granted by the government of Canada for the express purpose of encouraging the development of Canadian trade and the transportation of goods through Canadian channels.

This is an old standing difference between the Minister of Justice and myself. I have always said that this provision does not affect the Grand Trunk, because the Grand Trunk is not a party to that agreement.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Except in so far as they are guarantors of the second issue of bonds.

They are not a. party to this contract; they may guarantee bonds, but that does not render them liable to anv stipulations of the contract. I would not think the Grand Trunk Railway Company

could be made liable in any way under the stipulations of a contract to which it is not a party. It is quite true that therfe is a stipulation in the contract between the government and the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company by which the Grand Trunk Pacific Company undertakes that it shall procure the Grand Trunk Railway Company to guarantee its bonds. That does not, it seems to me, render the Grand Trunk Company liable to the stipulations of a contract to which it is not a party.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Except in so far as the Grand Trunk Company may be affected as the result of two things, as the result of their being guarantors of the second issue of bonds with respect to the western division, and also as the owners of $23,000,000 of the stock in this company. Anything that affects the Grand Trunk Pacific Company must necessarily, to a very large extent, affect the guarantors and stockholders.
Mr. R, L. BORDEN. It comes back exactly to what was said by the right hon. the Prime Minister (Sir Wilfrid Laurier), that he did not use the word * forfeit ' in a legal sense, but in a figurative or, to be more accurate, in a business sense, which is the sense now put forward by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Fitzpatrick).

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I think that was the meaning which was put on it when the matter was discussed last year.

Section 42 has not quite as much weight as it might have if it were not for the fact that according to the statement of Mr. Hays himself, the shipper routes from 75 to 80 per cent of the traffic. Now by the conditions thus imposed in the contract, only such grain as is not specifically routed by the shipper they are bound to carry. If the resolution that I proposed had been carried that all freight originating along the line and its tributaries should be carried over Canadian territory and through Canadian ports when it was intended for export abroad, you would have had a condition that would have meant something, but, today, according to the statement of Mr. Hays in the railway committee, a statement which was supported by the hon. member for West York (Mr. Campbell) at least from 75 to 80 per cent of the freight is routed by the shipper. The shipper, as has been pointed out again and again during the course cf this debate, is going to send his freight by the quickest route if he can do so just as cheaply as by the other route. Section 42 does not apply notwithstanding the fact that the right hon. Prime Minister and the hen. Minister of Justice claim that it does. Now, the hon. Minister of Justice also contends that the Grand Trunk Railway Company are bound, being guarantors of 25 per cent of the bonds, but the government are three-fold more strongly bound because they are guarantors of three-quarters of the bonds.

By the amendment, as I understand it, if the company default, this 25 per cent for which the company are the guarantors has to be redeemed proportionately with the three-quarters for which the country is responsible. So, we say that the guarantee, as far as the Grand Trunk Railway Company is concerned, is not even a moral guarantee, or a moral obligation such as the right hon. Prime Minister claims.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Business, not moral.

It is not business in any way. If it were business the company would be bound by the contract. It would be business to bind them by the contract if you can bind these people. We had a contract signed by all these titled gentlemen who are supposed to compose the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company, but it did not amount to much, because, after they had entered into a solemn bargain, they, for their own purposes^ broke it. What sort of a business or moral guarantee is it to say that these are the conditions on which hon. gentlemen opposite rely as being the conditions that are going to benefit the people, that are going to oblige the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company to carry this freight over Canadian soil and that are going to make these people pay three per cent interest on the money when they do not regard themselves bound by a contract in writing ? You have by your amended contract even less of a hold than you had previously in respect to this $25,000,000 of stock, because you allow them, under this amended contract, to dispose of the stock in the market. Every safeguard that was thrown around this transaction has been swept away. They were only poor safeguards, but even a poor safeguard is better than none at all. So completely do the government appear to be in the power of these Grand Trunk people, and that is the way that any common sense business man will look at it, that they have conceded everything to them. The hon. Minister of Finance during the by-election in the county of Hochelaga declared that the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company must come to their terms or they would build the road themselves, but after all his violent abuse and defiance, when he and his friends had looked over the ground, when they had received the returns from the managers of that election, when they found that it was absolutely necessary to the success of the government candidate on that occasion to have the undivided Grand Trunk vote, that lion gentleman came down. Hon. gentlemen opposite were willing to modify their views because the right hon. leader of the government knew what a serious blow it would be to the prestige of his government to lose a by-election in Quebec. It was bad enough to lose an election in the maritime provinces, bad enough to have increased majorities recorded

against them in the province of Ontario but, in the right hon. gentleman's own province of Quebec, which in the general elections had given him such a large majority, to lose a by-election would be altogether too great a blow to his government and so he was willing to give way to the demands of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company. Now, Sir, it does seem to me that we have a very poor guarantee that these conditions will be fulfilled.

It is my painful, Mr. Speaker, my very painful duty, to have to announce the death of one of our colleagues, in the person of William F. McCreary. The circumstances of the death of Mr. McCreary are all the more sad that they come so unexpectedly upon us. In many ways they recall those of the death of Mr. Cargill only last session. Like Mr. Cargill, Mr. McCreary was apparently in the best of health to the last moment, and indeed only yesterday was engaged with us in debate and defending bis opinions on a most important question. While thus addressing the House the hand of death was already upon him, which shows how true it is that we are only shadow's and in pursuit only of shadows. I am sure that Mr. McCreary had on both sides of the House only friends. He was of an ardent temperament, defended his opinions with vigour, and at all times enjoyed the keenness of debate, but there was no more kind hearted man in the House. Even those who did not share his opinions, respected his views and cherished his kindly disposition. We have had many evidences, since the news of his death spread through the House, that on the other side as well as this the feeling of mourning is very deep. It is not the custom of the House to adjourn for the death of a colleague. As a rule, the death of a colleague, even the most eminent, has not prevented the House going on with business ; but the circumstances in this case are so particularly painful, that no one in the chamber will feel disposed to proceed with the business now engaging our attention and in which our colleague took a prominent and active part. The disposition will be rather that we should adjourn our debate instead of proceeding any further with the discussion in which we are now engaged. I beg therefore to move, seconded by Mr. Sproule, that the House do now adjourn.

In the absence of the hon. the leader of the opposition, and on behalf of this side of the House, I desire to express our sorrowful concurrence in what has been said by the

right hon, the leader of the government. The untimely death of a colleague is at all times mournful and overshadows not only this House but the part of the country which he represents ; but it is marked with additional sadness when, as in this instance, one who was in the prime of life only yesterday, taking part in the active duties of his position, is so suddenly called from among us and we shall know him no more for ever. On behalf of this side of the House, I can bear testimony that we always found the late Mr. McCreary a most sociable, genial and kind hearted man, attentive to his duties, assiduous at his work, and always endeavouring faithfully to represent his people and work in the best interests of his country. We oil this side had not the same opportunities of knowing him that the right hon. the leader of the government and his friends had, but in every capacity in which we were brought in contact with him, we always found him a man of most genial disposition, kindly at heart and always the gentleman. These unfortunate events in human life, especially in conriec-tion with parliamentary life, have been all too frequent of late years. The right hon. the leader of the government spok* of the circumstances of the untimely death of our late colleague Mr. Cargill, and in this morning's papers we have the announcement of the death of one of our colleagues in the upper House, Senator Reid, of British Columbia, a very respected gentleman. with whom I became acquainted years ago and whom I knew well up to the time of his sickness, and who was only known to be respected. I am sure that I express the sentiments of all on this side when I say that our tenderest sympathy and condolence go out to the bereaved family of Mr. McCreary and his friends in the constituency he represented. I may say that these sad occurrences sometimes tend to do away with the asperities of public life and ought to make us at least more kindly disposed to each other. It is in my judgment fitting that this House should adjourn out of respect for the memory of our departed colleague, and to express the sympathy we feel for the bereaved ones left behind. I beg to second the motion.

speakeroldname: Hon. CLIFFORD SIFTON (Minister of the Interior).
speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I desire, Mr. Speaker, the privilege of adding a few words to what has been already said upon the painful occasion of the death of our fellow member. My acquaintanceship with Mr. McCreary extended perhaps over a period greater than that of any other member of the House. It js now some twenty-four years since be and I were law students together in the city of M innipeg. After he began the practice of his profession, lie attained a considerable degree of prominence in connection with municipal affairs and was ultimately elected mayor of the city of Winnipeg, which Mr. SPROULE.
may be taken as an illustration of the esteem in which he was regarded by his fellow-citizens among whom he had lived a considerable number of years. I was inexpressibly shocked an hour or so ago when I received a message that, owing to the fact that he had not appeared during the day, it was found necessary to force open the door of his room, when the sad truth was learned. He was with me yesterday in the afternoon an hour and a-hall' discussing various matters of interest to his constituency and later on in the evening, after he had addressed the House a few minutes upon the Railway Bill, he again asked me to go to my room and we there discussed matters connected with his constituency. I remember remarking that I never saw him look so well or enjoying such good spirits. Mr. McCreary sometimes expressed doubts about the advisability of continuing in his political career, but during the last, couple of days, on one or two occasions when I saw him, he expressed himself as having rather made up his mind, for the present at least, to continue in political life. Those who knew him will agree that few men were better adapted for a political career. He was a man of ability, strength of character and particularly well able to express his views in a vigorous and convincing manner.
I suppose that if I had been asked last evening to say who, of the members of the House of Commons, would be the least likely to be the subject of such a sad occurrence, the name of Mr. McCreary is the one that would probably have suggested itself to my mind. As one of his colleagues from the province of Manitoba, I feel that it is only proper for me to express the esteem in which he was held by the representatives from his own province and the Northwest Territories, and at the same time to express my sincere sympathy with his family in the very sad bereavement which they have sustained. I can hardly yet realize, Mr. Speaker, the fact that this friend and colleague was with me last evening, was in my room at eleven o'clock, left there to enter the House and an hour later retired to his hotel, and that only an hour ago I was called upon to witness the fact that he had passed away. When we think of the feelings which we experience under such circumstances, we can, perhaps, in a faint degree, realize the feelings of those who were bound to him by closer ties.
Motion agreed to, and House adjourned at 8.45 p.m.
